new_statements.quote: 2.3 Tones. The following tones are distinguished as phonemic units: High (H) ... Low (L) ... High-falling (HF) ... Low-falling (LF) ... In addition there is a high-rising tone, restricted to polar questions [p. 23] ... Finally, there is a tonal downstep (marked with a preceding exclamation mark), whereby a word or part of a word is pronounced at a lower tone level than the preceding part. Stress, or pitch accent, clearly exists but does not appear to phonologically distinctive. [p. 25, sic]
new_statements.citation: König, Christa, Bernd Heine & Karsten Legère. 2015. The Akie Language of Tanzania: A Sketch of Discourse Grammar. (Studies in Nilotic Linguistics 9.) Tokyo: ILCAA, Tokyo University of Foreign Studies.
new_statements.locator: Ch. 2 'Notes on phonology', section 2.3 'Tones', p. 25 (last sentence of the section; PDF p. 35); tone inventory p. 23
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Akie is described as a tone language with four phonemic tones (high, low, high-falling, low-falling) plus downstep; the authors state that stress (or pitch accent) exists phonetically but is not phonologically distinctive. They give no rule for where it falls; their narrow phonetic transcriptions mark a stress ˈ whose position varies across words (initial in [ˈʔàmdɪ̀] 'food', [ˈkárɪkà] 'woman', [ˈnáːpɪ́ʃànà] 'seven'; second syllable in [kàˈlíːsyà] 'Kalisya', [wàˈárɛ̀ː] 'children', [ʔàˈŋkûn] 'I know'), without discussion.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the authors explicitly decline to treat context-sensitive tonal variation ('cannot be treated here') and say nothing further about stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the word-level phonology in general ('Notes on phonology' restricted to an inventory of phonological and tonological units); no distinction of citation vs. phrase forms is made for stress. Variety: Akie of Gitu/Kibirashi, Kilindi District (Tanga Region), fieldwork 2013-2014; authors say the language has no noticeable dialects.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Akie (glottocode mosi1247, ISO mwy; also known as Mósiro / '(N)dorobo') as spoken around Gitu and Kibirashi, Kilindi District, Tanga Region, north-central Tanzania (fieldwork 2013-2014, main consultants Bahati Nkuyaki and Nkoiseyyo Kalisya); the authors state the language is fairly homogeneous with no dialects. Not to be confused with Kenyan Okiek (okie1245).

sources.note: Ch. 2 'Notes on phonology' (pp. 17-25): four phonemic tones (H, L, high-falling, low-falling) plus downstep; section 2.3 ends (p. 25): 'Stress, or pitch accent, clearly exists but does not appear to phonologically distinctive.' No stress position is stated; phonetic transcriptions carry a stress mark ˈ in varying positions (e.g. [ˈʔàmdɪ̀] 'food', [kàˈlíːsyà] 'Kalisya', [ˈkárɪkà] 'woman', [wàˈárɛ̀ː] 'children') without comment.
